prompt:
A 49-year-old man is 3 years out from a deceased-donor kidney transplant (baseline creatinine 1.3) on tacrolimus 3 mg twice daily (usual trough 5 to 7 ng/mL), mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg twice daily, and prednisone 5 mg daily. Urgent care started clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily 6 days ago for sinusitis. He now has hand tremor, headache, and poor appetite. BP 158/94. Labs: creatinine 2.2, potassium 5.9, magnesium 1.3, glucose 238, tacrolimus trough 24 ng/mL. Urinalysis is bland and ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis. His sinus symptoms are much better. How would you manage this?

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Recognize clarithromycin inhibition of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein as the cause of the supratherapeutic tacrolimus level and nephrotoxicity.
Stop clarithromycin immediately.
Hold tacrolimus until the trough falls toward target, then resume at a dose guided by levels.
Repeat properly timed tacrolimus trough levels every 24 to 48 hours until back in range.
Notify and coordinate with the transplant nephrology team the same day.
If further antibacterial therapy is needed for sinusitis, use a non-interacting agent such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or doxycycline.
Continue mycophenolate and prednisone while tacrolimus is held.
Treat the hyperkalemia with dietary restriction and a potassium binder as needed.
Obtain an ECG.
Replete magnesium.
Monitor glucose and check hemoglobin A1c, treating hyperglycemia if it persists.
Recheck creatinine and electrolytes every 1 to 2 days until improving.
Pursue transplant kidney biopsy if creatinine does not return toward baseline after tacrolimus levels normalize.
Check donor-specific antibodies if creatinine fails to improve.
Check BK virus PCR if creatinine fails to improve.
Ensure adequate hydration and avoid other nephrotoxins.
If blood pressure stays elevated, favor a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine.
Counsel him to check with the transplant team or pharmacist before any new medication, supplement, or grapefruit product.
Add a tacrolimus interaction alert to his pharmacy and medication records.
Assess for features of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome such as visual change, confusion, or seizure, and escalate urgently if present.
Continue clarithromycin to finish the course while lowering the tacrolimus dose.
Switch clarithromycin to erythromycin.
Continue tacrolimus at the same dose and recheck in 2 weeks.
Stop all immunosuppression, including mycophenolate and prednisone.
Tell him to stop tacrolimus indefinitely until his next routine clinic visit.
Resume the full prior tacrolimus dose immediately after stopping clarithromycin regardless of the level.
Permanently convert tacrolimus to cyclosporine.
Start diltiazem or verapamil for blood pressure.
Start an ACE inhibitor or ARB now despite hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury.
Give NSAIDs for his headache.
Order contrast-enhanced CT to evaluate the acute kidney injury.
Perform an immediate allograft biopsy before correcting the tacrolimus level.
Treat empirically for acute rejection with pulse methylprednisolone.
Start plasmapheresis empirically.
Give intravenous immunoglobulin empirically.
Start carbamazepine for the tremor.
Increase the mycophenolate dose to compensate for holding tacrolimus.
Give large-volume intravenous fluids to flush the kidney despite hypertension.
Use a 2-hour post-dose tacrolimus level to guide dosing.
